title: A Cross-Modal Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensate Material Properties and Cellular Function Across Species and Perturbations
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates formed by phase separation are quintessential mesoscale structures whose emergent material properties (viscosity, elasticity, interfacial tension, aging) shape gene regulation, signaling, and stress responses. Yet the field remains fragmented: biophysical measurements are reported in disparate experimental systems, while large-scale imaging, proteomics, and genetics datasets rarely connect condensate material state to cellular outcomes. This working group will synthesize publicly available datasets to build a unified, cross-species map linking condensate composition and sequence features to emergent material properties and downstream phenotypes.

We will integrate (i) curated condensate component databases (e.g., LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS), (ii) protein sequence/structure annotations (AlphaFold DB, InterPro, disorder predictors, prion-like domain catalogs), (iii) high-content microscopy repositories and segmentation-ready image sets (Cell Painting, Image Data Resource, Human Protein Atlas subcellular localization, yeast GFP collections), (iv) proteomics and interactomics (PRIDE, BioGRID, HuRI), and (v) perturbation-response resources (DepMap CRISPR screens, GEO/ArrayExpress transcriptomics, LINCS). We will extract quantitative condensate phenotypes from images using reproducible pipelines (CellProfiler/napari + deep learning segmentation) and harmonize them with reported rheology/FRAP-derived metrics from the literature via text-mining and manual curation.

The core scientific questions are: (1) Which molecular features (valency, charge patterning, aromatic content, disorder architecture, multimerization) best predict condensate material state across contexts? (2) Do distinct “material property regimes” correspond to conserved functional outputs (e.g., transcriptional bursts, stress granule-mediated translation control) and pathological transitions (e.g., solidification in neurodegeneration)? (3) Can we identify universal versus lineage-specific design principles for mesoscale organization?

Methodologically, we will develop multimodal machine learning models that jointly embed sequence/structure, interaction networks, and image-derived condensate morphology to predict material properties and phenotypic consequences. We will emphasize interpretable models (e.g., graph neural networks with attention over interaction motifs; sparse additive models over sequence features) to generate testable hypotheses. Benchmark tasks and open evaluation sets will be released to spur community contributions.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated expertise spanning polymer physics, cell biology, computer vision, NLP-based literature mining, and statistical learning, plus the infrastructure to host community curation sprints and model hackathons. The working group will include experimentalists who understand assay biases, data scientists to build harmonization pipelines, and theorists to connect emergent properties to mesoscale physics.

Training will be embedded via trainee-led “data carpentry” modules on image analysis, reproducible ML, and open curation, culminating in a public, versioned knowledge graph of condensate properties and an open-source toolkit to relate condensate material state to cellular function. Outputs will follow open science practices: containerized workflows, FAIR metadata schemas, and pre-registered analysis plans to ensure reproducibility and broad reuse.

title: Emergent Principles of Organelle Contact Sites: A Synthesis of Proteomics, Imaging, and Genetic Interaction Data
abstract:
Membrane contact sites (MCS) between organelles (ER–mitochondria, ER–endosome, mitochondria–lysosome, etc.) are mesoscale hubs for lipid transfer, calcium signaling, and organelle dynamics. Despite rapid discovery of tethering proteins and lipid transporters, fundamental questions remain: What network architectures make MCS robust? Which molecular features predict contact specificity? How do contacts rewire under stress and disease? Addressing these requires synthesis across proteomics, imaging, and functional genomics—data that exist publicly but are rarely integrated.

This working group will assemble and harmonize diverse datasets: (i) proximity labeling proteomics (BioID/APEX datasets in PRIDE) targeting organelle membranes and known MCS components, (ii) subcellular localization and co-localization imaging (Human Protein Atlas, IDR, yeast GFP libraries), (iii) organelle morphology and dynamics from high-content screens (Cell Painting, Mitobank-like imaging sets), (iv) genetic interaction maps (yeast GI networks, DepMap coessentiality), and (v) lipidomics and metabolomics studies that report contact-dependent flux phenotypes (Metabolomics Workbench). We will create a standardized ontology for contact site types, experimental modalities, and confidence levels, enabling cross-study comparisons.

Scientific aims: (1) Infer a conserved “contactome” by building probabilistic networks of MCS proteins and their organelle-pair specificity across species. (2) Identify emergent network motifs (redundant tethers, modular lipid-transfer units, stress-inducible adapters) that confer robustness to perturbations. (3) Link MCS network states to higher-order phenotypes such as mitochondrial fission/fusion balance, lysosomal positioning, and unfolded protein responses, using integrated imaging and transcriptomic readouts.

Analytically, we will develop multi-layer network models that combine physical proximity evidence (proximity proteomics), functional coupling (genetic interactions/coessentiality), and spatial co-localization (image-derived metrics). We will apply community detection and dynamic network inference to detect condition-specific rewiring. To address heterogeneity and batch effects, we will use hierarchical Bayesian models and domain adaptation methods for imaging features. Interpretability will be prioritized to yield mechanistic hypotheses (e.g., predicting which tethers compensate for loss of a lipid transporter in specific cell states).

NCEMS resources are critical to convene organelle biologists, mass spectrometrists, imaging experts, network scientists, and statisticians to agree on standards, curate metadata, and build shared pipelines. The project exceeds single-lab capacity because it requires cross-modal harmonization, extensive curation of experimental context, and robust benchmarking across organisms and cell types.

Deliverables will include an open, queryable MCS knowledge graph; reproducible workflows for integrating proximity proteomics with imaging and genetics; and a set of predictive models linking contact-site composition to organelle phenotypes. Training components will include trainee-led annotation jamborees, tutorials on network inference and image feature extraction, and open challenges to engage new talent. All code, derived datasets, and documentation will be released under permissive licenses with full provenance tracking.

title: A Pan-Cell Atlas of Cytoskeletal Self-Organization: Integrating Live-Cell Imaging, Proteomics, and Biophysical Models
abstract:
The cytoskeleton is a paradigmatic emergent system: local interactions among actin, microtubules, motors, and crosslinkers generate mesoscale structures (stress fibers, asters, cortical networks) that determine cell shape, division, and migration. While thousands of imaging experiments and perturbation datasets exist, we lack a synthesis that connects molecular composition and regulation to emergent cytoskeletal architectures across cell types and conditions.

This working group will integrate publicly available resources spanning (i) live-cell imaging repositories (Image Data Resource, Cell Image Library) containing actin/microtubule reporters and perturbations, (ii) high-content morphological profiling (Cell Painting) that captures cytoskeleton-dependent shape features, (iii) proteomics of cytoskeletal fractions and interactomes (PRIDE, BioGRID), (iv) phosphorylation and signaling datasets relevant to cytoskeletal regulation (PhosphoSitePlus, CPTAC), and (v) CRISPR/RNAi perturbation screens affecting migration, adhesion, and cytokinesis (DepMap, genome-wide RNAi datasets). We will build standardized pipelines to extract quantitative descriptors of cytoskeletal organization from images (filament orientation fields, network anisotropy, bundle thickness, dynamic instability proxies) using computer vision and biophysical feature engineering.

Key questions: (1) What molecular “control knobs” (motor abundance, crosslinker type, post-translational modifications) most strongly determine emergent cytoskeletal patterns? (2) Are there universal low-dimensional “states” of cytoskeletal organization shared across cell types, or are patterns strongly context-specific? (3) Can we predict transitions between states (e.g., lamellipodial to contractile) from upstream signaling and protein composition?

We will develop integrative models that combine image-derived cytoskeletal metrics with omics features using representation learning and causal inference. A central methodological contribution will be bridging data-driven embeddings with mechanistic active gel and polymerization models: we will fit simplified biophysical models to observed mesoscale patterns, enabling interpretable parameters (effective contractility, polymerization rate, crosslinking strength) to be inferred from imaging at scale. This “mechanistic latent space” will allow cross-dataset comparisons even when imaging modalities differ.

NCEMS support is needed to coordinate multidisciplinary expertise—cell biophysicists, imaging analysts, ML researchers, and statisticians—to create community standards for cytoskeletal feature extraction and to host collaborative model-fitting sprints. The scale of harmonizing diverse imaging modalities and linking them to proteomic and perturbation data exceeds typical lab capabilities.

Outputs will include an open Cytoskeletal Self-Organization Atlas with harmonized features, metadata, and embeddings; containerized workflows for image-to-physics parameter inference; and predictive models linking molecular perturbations to emergent architectures and cellular behaviors. Training will be delivered through hands-on workshops on reproducible imaging analysis, mechanistic modeling, and multimodal data integration, with trainees leading benchmark dataset creation and documentation. All results will be disseminated openly, enabling broad reuse and accelerating discovery of general principles of cytoskeletal emergence.

title: Emergent Chromatin Domains at the Mesoscale: Synthesizing Hi-C, Imaging, and Epigenomic Data to Explain 3D Genome Function
abstract:
Chromatin folds into mesoscale structures—loops, topologically associating domains (TADs), compartments, and transcriptional hubs—that exhibit emergent behavior not predictable from individual DNA-binding events. Although vast public datasets exist (Hi-C and derivatives, ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, imaging), fundamental puzzles persist: Which molecular mechanisms are necessary and sufficient for domain formation? How do domains relate to transcriptional variability, replication timing, and genome stability across cell types and species?

This working group will synthesize (i) 3D genome conformation datasets (4D Nucleome, GEO Hi-C/Micro-C, Capture-C), (ii) super-resolution and multiplexed imaging of chromatin organization (4DN imaging, IDR), (iii) epigenomic profiles (ENCODE/Roadmap ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq), (iv) single-cell multi-omics (scATAC+scRNA, scHi-C where available), and (v) perturbation datasets targeting cohesin/CTCF, chromatin remodelers, and transcription machinery (CRISPR screens, degron time courses in GEO). We will harmonize metadata (cell cycle state, differentiation stage, perturbation timing) and implement standardized processing pipelines to generate comparable domain calls and imaging-derived spatial metrics.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify conserved versus context-specific rules linking epigenomic patterns to emergent 3D domains. (2) Quantify how perturbations shift domain boundaries and compartmentalization, and how these shifts propagate to gene expression variability and replication timing. (3) Test competing mechanistic models—loop extrusion, compartmental phase separation, transcription-driven clustering—by fitting them to cross-modal observations and evaluating predictive performance.

Methodologically, we will build a model comparison framework in which mechanistic simulations (polymer models with extrusion and compartment interactions) are calibrated using summary statistics derived from Hi-C and imaging. We will pair this with machine learning predictors that map 1D epigenomic tracks to 3D organization, using interpretable architectures (e.g., attention over regulatory elements, graph models over genomic bins). A key innovation will be integrating imaging constraints to reduce identifiability issues inherent in Hi-C-only inference.

NCEMS support is essential because the work requires coordinated expertise in polymer physics, genomics, imaging, and statistics, plus community agreement on standards for cross-study domain comparisons. The project’s scale—processing hundreds of datasets, curating perturbation metadata, and running model-fitting pipelines—demands dedicated synthesis infrastructure and collaborative working sessions.

Deliverables will include an open benchmark suite for 3D genome model evaluation; harmonized, analysis-ready matrices and imaging-derived metrics; and a public “Mechanisms of Chromatin Domains” resource with reproducible workflows. Training will be incorporated through trainee-led reproducibility audits, tutorials on 3D genome processing, and open-source contributions to simulation and ML toolkits. The synthesis will yield deeper, more generalizable insights into how mesoscale chromatin organization emerges and controls nuclear function.

title: A Unified Synthesis of Protein Complex Stoichiometry and Assembly Pathways from Structural, Proteomic, and Ribosome Profiling Data
abstract:
Cells rely on thousands of protein complexes whose emergent functions depend on correct stoichiometry and assembly order. Despite abundant public data—structures, interaction maps, quantitative proteomics, and translation dynamics—we lack an integrated understanding of how assembly pathways and dosage constraints shape complex composition across conditions and species. This working group will build a synthesis framework to infer complex stoichiometry control principles and predict assembly vulnerabilities.

We will integrate (i) structural repositories (PDB, AlphaFold DB, EMDB) to define interfaces and assembly intermediates, (ii) curated complex catalogs (CORUM, Complex Portal), (iii) quantitative proteomics across tissues and perturbations (PRIDE, CPTAC), (iv) ribosome profiling and translation initiation datasets (GWIPS-viz-linked studies in GEO), (v) chaperone interaction and co-translational assembly evidence (BioGRID, proximity labeling proteomics), and (vi) genetic dependency/interaction data (DepMap, yeast GI). Harmonization will include mapping orthologs, standardizing protein identifiers, and annotating complex membership confidence.

Core questions: (1) What global rules govern complex stoichiometry—are there conserved “dosage buffering” strategies across complex types (ribosomes, proteasomes, membrane complexes)? (2) Can we infer assembly order from co-translational interaction signals, interface topology, and translation timing, and how does this differ across organisms? (3) Which complexes are most sensitive to subunit imbalance, and can we predict disease-relevant vulnerabilities (e.g., haploinsufficiency, aneuploidy effects)?

Analytical approach: We will develop probabilistic models that combine structural interface graphs with quantitative abundance and translation-rate data to infer latent assembly pathways and stoichiometric constraints. Network flow and Bayesian structure learning will be used to rank plausible assembly orders consistent with co-translational evidence. We will also build predictive models linking inferred imbalance sensitivity to genetic dependency patterns and proteostasis stress signatures.

NCEMS support is required because the project spans structural biology, proteomics, translation biology, and statistical modeling, and demands coordinated curation and scalable computation. No single lab typically has access to the breadth of expertise needed to reconcile structural interface information with proteome-wide quantitative constraints.

Deliverables: (i) an open “Complex Assembly Atlas” with inferred stoichiometries, assembly pathway hypotheses, and confidence scores; (ii) reproducible pipelines for integrating structure, proteomics, and ribosome profiling; (iii) benchmarks for assembly inference methods; and (iv) case studies on medically relevant complexes (mitochondrial OXPHOS, spliceosome, chromatin remodelers). Training will include workshops on proteomics harmonization, structural data parsing, and Bayesian modeling, with trainees leading curation of specific complex families. All outputs will be released openly with versioned datasets and transparent provenance, enabling the community to test and refine emergent principles of complex assembly.

title: Mesoscale Metabolic Channeling: Synthesizing Spatial Proteomics, Metabolomics, and Enzyme Complex Data to Map Functional Microdomains
abstract:
Metabolism is often depicted as a well-mixed network, yet growing evidence suggests enzymes form mesoscale assemblies and microdomains that enable metabolic channeling—emergent behavior where spatial organization alters flux, noise, and regulation. Public datasets now include spatial proteomics, organelle proteomes, metabolomics, and interaction maps, but they are rarely integrated to test when and where channeling occurs and what design principles govern it.

This working group will synthesize (i) spatial proteomics and subcellular fractionation datasets (Human Protein Atlas spatial proteomics, PRIDE fractionation studies), (ii) proximity labeling proteomics for metabolic enzymes (PRIDE), (iii) metabolomics across compartments and perturbations (Metabolomics Workbench, HMDB-linked studies), (iv) protein complex and interaction data (CORUM, BioGRID), (v) imaging-based localization for metabolic enzymes (IDR, HPA immunofluorescence), and (vi) genome-scale metabolic models and flux datasets (BiGG, published 13C MFA datasets with shared raw data). We will curate evidence for enzyme co-localization, complex formation, and condition dependence.

Scientific questions: (1) Which pathways exhibit strongest signatures of channeling (e.g., glycolysis, purine synthesis, TCA-associated metabolons), and are these conserved across taxa? (2) How do stress, cell cycle, or differentiation alter metabolic microdomain organization? (3) Can spatial organization explain discrepancies between enzyme abundance and observed metabolite levels or fluxes?

Methodological innovations will include constructing “spatially annotated metabolic networks” where edges are weighted by co-localization and complex evidence, enabling simulations that compare well-mixed versus microdomain-constrained flux. We will develop statistical tests for channeling signatures using metabolite covariance patterns and perturbation responses, and integrate imaging/proteomics priors to constrain model space. Machine learning will be used to predict microdomain formation propensity from enzyme features (oligomerization, disorder, membrane association) and interaction network context.

NCEMS support is essential to convene metabolomics experts, systems biologists, proteomics specialists, and biophysicists to align on standards for spatial evidence and to build interoperable pipelines across omics modalities. The project’s scope—harmonizing metabolomics metadata, mapping metabolites across platforms, and integrating with localization and interaction data—requires dedicated synthesis infrastructure.

Deliverables will include an open atlas of candidate metabolic microdomains with evidence scores; reproducible workflows for mapping metabolites and spatial proteomics into compartment-resolved models; and a set of community benchmarks for detecting channeling from public data. Training will be provided through hands-on modules on metabolomics normalization, network modeling, and FAIR data practices, with trainees leading pathway-focused curation efforts. The synthesis will advance understanding of emergent metabolic behavior arising from mesoscale spatial organization.

title: Emergent Robustness in Gene Regulatory Networks: A Synthesis of Single-Cell Perturbation Atlases Across Cell Types
abstract:
Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) display emergent robustness: stable cell identities persist despite molecular noise and many perturbations, yet can switch catastrophically under others. Single-cell perturbation technologies have generated large public datasets (CRISPRi/a Perturb-seq, CROP-seq, multimodal readouts), but the field lacks a cross-study synthesis to identify universal robustness motifs and context-specific vulnerabilities.

This working group will integrate publicly available single-cell perturbation datasets from GEO, ArrayExpress, and dedicated portals (e.g., scPerturb resources), including CRISPR-based knockdowns/activations with scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, and protein readouts (CITE-seq). We will harmonize gene identifiers, perturbation efficacies, cell state annotations, and batch effects using standardized pipelines. We will also integrate transcription factor binding/epigenomic priors (ENCODE) and protein interaction networks (BioGRID) to constrain GRN inference.

Key questions: (1) What network motifs (feedback loops, redundant regulators, feedforward motifs) repeatedly underlie robustness across diverse cell types? (2) Which perturbations cause state transitions versus buffered responses, and can we predict this from network topology and chromatin context? (3) How do emergent properties like multistability and criticality vary across differentiation trajectories and disease states?

Analytical plan: We will infer GRNs using a combination of causal inference methods tailored to perturbation data (e.g., conditional independence with intervention labels, dynamical latent variable models) and compare inferred networks across datasets via alignment techniques. We will quantify robustness using metrics such as response sparsity, attractor stability, and variance amplification. A methodological deliverable will be a benchmarking framework that evaluates GRN inference methods on real perturbation data with standardized gold-standard proxies (e.g., TF binding, curated pathways) and reproducible splits.

NCEMS support is required because meaningful synthesis demands coordination across many datasets with heterogeneous protocols and readouts, and requires expertise spanning single-cell genomics, statistics, dynamical systems, and computational infrastructure. The working group format enables community consensus on metadata standards (perturbation annotation, efficacy reporting) and fosters broad participation.

Deliverables will include: (i) a harmonized cross-study perturbation atlas with unified cell state labels; (ii) an open library of robustness metrics and visualization tools; (iii) a catalog of conserved robustness motifs and predicted “tipping-point” regulators; and (iv) tutorials and reproducible notebooks for trainees. Training will focus on best practices for single-cell data integration, causal modeling, and open science workflows. By synthesizing intervention-rich datasets, the project will reveal emergent principles governing stability and change in cellular regulatory systems.

title: A Community Synthesis of Mesoscale Protein Quality Control: Integrating Proteostasis Networks, Aggregation Data, and Stress Responses
abstract:
Protein quality control (PQC) is an emergent cellular system spanning chaperones, proteasomes, autophagy, and stress granules. Failures in PQC lead to aggregation and disease, yet we lack a unified synthesis connecting proteostasis network states to aggregation propensity and cell fate across organisms and stressors. Public datasets now include proteome-wide aggregation measurements, chaperone interactomes, stress transcriptomics, and imaging of aggregates—ripe for integrative analysis.

This working group will synthesize (i) proteomics datasets quantifying insoluble/aggregated fractions under stress (PRIDE), (ii) interactomes for chaperones and ubiquitin ligases (BioGRID, HuRI), (iii) transcriptomic responses to heat shock, oxidative stress, and proteasome inhibition (GEO), (iv) imaging datasets of aggregate formation and clearance (IDR, Cell Image Library), (v) genetic screens for proteostasis factors (DepMap, yeast screens), and (vi) sequence/structure features (AlphaFold, disorder predictions, aggregation propensity predictors). We will curate stress conditions, time courses, and cell types to enable comparative analyses.

Scientific questions: (1) Can we define discrete, reproducible “proteostasis states” that predict whether cells route misfolded proteins to degradation, sequestration, or refolding? (2) Which network configurations confer resilience (rapid recovery) versus vulnerability (runaway aggregation)? (3) How do mesoscale assemblies (stress granules, aggresomes) interact with PQC pathways to create emergent thresholds and hysteresis?

Methodologically, we will develop integrative models combining network biology and time-series analysis. Latent state models will infer proteostasis regimes from multi-omics signatures. We will link these regimes to aggregate imaging phenotypes and insoluble proteome composition. Causal discovery approaches leveraging perturbation screens will identify key control nodes. A specific methodological product will be an open pipeline for harmonizing “insoluble proteome” assays and mapping proteins across studies with standardized confidence metrics.

NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis spans many data types and requires deep domain expertise to interpret assay-specific biases (e.g., detergent solubility differences). The collaboration will include neurodegeneration experts, proteomics analysts, imaging scientists, and computational modelers to ensure robust integration.

Deliverables: an open Proteostasis Emergence Atlas cataloging stress conditions, proteostasis states, aggregate compositions, and predicted control nodes; reproducible workflows for integrating insoluble proteomics with imaging and transcriptomics; and community benchmarks for predicting aggregation outcomes from sequence and network context. Training will include trainee-led curation of stress datasets, workshops on reproducible proteomics and imaging analysis, and open-source contributions. The project will illuminate emergent PQC behavior and identify general principles of cellular resilience.

title: Emergent Cell Polarity from Molecular Interactions: Synthesizing Spatial Transcriptomics, Proteomics, and Imaging Across Epithelia
abstract:
Cell polarity is an emergent property in which local molecular interactions generate stable, large-scale spatial organization (apical–basal domains, tight junctions) that enables tissue function. While many polarity regulators are known, we lack a cross-tissue synthesis connecting molecular composition and signaling to emergent polarity architectures, especially across development, disease, and species. Public spatial omics and imaging datasets now make this synthesis feasible.

This working group will integrate (i) spatial transcriptomics datasets (10x Visium and other platforms with public releases in GEO and portals), (ii) single-cell RNA-seq atlases with epithelial annotations (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens), (iii) proteomics of junctional complexes and membrane domains (PRIDE), (iv) imaging datasets of epithelial polarity markers (Human Protein Atlas, IDR), and (v) perturbation datasets affecting polarity (CRISPR screens, organoid perturbation transcriptomics). We will focus on harmonizing epithelial cell type ontologies and spatial coordinate frameworks to compare polarity programs across tissues.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify conserved “polarity modules” (gene/protein sets) and quantify their spatial segregation across epithelia. (2) Determine how emergent polarity breaks down in cancer, inflammation, and infection by comparing spatial organization signatures. (3) Link molecular modules to mesoscale structures such as tight junction continuity, lumen formation, and planar cell polarity patterns.

Analytical approach: We will develop computational methods to infer polarity axes and domain boundaries from spatial transcriptomics and multiplex imaging, using spatial statistics and graph-based segmentation. Multi-omic factor models will integrate RNA, protein, and imaging features to define polarity states. We will also incorporate known interaction networks to interpret modules mechanistically. A methodological contribution will be an open “polarity scoring” toolkit that quantifies polarity strength and organization from diverse spatial datasets.

NCEMS support is required to convene developmental biologists, epithelial physiologists, spatial omics experts, and computational scientists to align on ontologies, quality control, and cross-platform integration. The project goes beyond a single lab due to the breadth of tissues, platforms, and the need for rigorous standardization.

Deliverables will include a cross-tissue Polarity Synthesis Atlas with harmonized spatial datasets, polarity scores, and module annotations; reproducible pipelines for spatial data integration; and a catalog of disease-associated polarity disruption signatures. Training will be embedded through workshops on spatial data analysis, open annotation of epithelial structures, and reproducibility practices. This synthesis will advance understanding of how mesoscale polarity emerges from molecular networks and how its disruption drives pathology.

title: A Synthesis of Mitochondrial Network Emergence: Linking Morphodynamics, Proteostasis, and Bioenergetics Across Cell Types
abstract:
Mitochondria form dynamic networks whose emergent morphology—fragmented, tubular, or hyperfused—reflects the balance of fission, fusion, transport, and mitophagy. Although many public datasets measure mitochondrial morphology, gene dependencies, proteomics, and respiration, they remain siloed. This working group will synthesize these resources to uncover general principles linking molecular regulation to emergent mitochondrial network states and cellular outcomes.

We will integrate (i) high-content imaging datasets with mitochondrial stains/reporters (Cell Painting, IDR), (ii) curated mitochondrial protein resources (MitoCarta), (iii) proteomics and phosphoproteomics under metabolic and stress perturbations (CPTAC, PRIDE), (iv) CRISPR dependency data for mitochondrial genes (DepMap), (v) transcriptomic responses to metabolic shifts (GEO), and (vi) publicly available bioenergetic measurements where raw data are shared (Seahorse-style outputs in supplementary repositories). Image analysis pipelines will extract network features (branch length distributions, connectivity, fragmentation indices) and, where time-lapse exists, morphodynamic rates.

Scientific questions: (1) Are there conserved, low-dimensional mitochondrial “network states” that recur across cell types and perturbations? (2) Which molecular programs (post-translational modifications of DRP1/OPA1, proteostasis pathways, lipid metabolism) drive transitions between states? (3) How do emergent network states predict higher-order phenotypes such as apoptosis sensitivity, ROS handling, and differentiation potential?

Analytically, we will build multimodal models that link omics signatures to image-derived network states, using domain adaptation to handle different imaging conditions. We will combine mechanistic modeling (balance equations for fission/fusion/turnover) with data-driven inference to estimate effective rates from snapshots and limited time series. We will also identify genetic interaction patterns that reveal compensatory pathways stabilizing network morphology.

NCEMS support is essential due to the scale of imaging harmonization and the need to integrate across modalities and institutions. The working group will bring together mitochondrial biologists, quantitative microscopists, ML experts, and systems biologists to establish community standards for mitochondrial network quantification.

Deliverables include an open MitoNetwork Emergence Atlas with standardized morphology features, inferred network states, and linked molecular predictors; reproducible image analysis and integration workflows; and a set of prioritized hypotheses about regulators that control state transitions across contexts. Training will include trainee-led development of annotation sets for benchmarking segmentation, tutorials on reproducible image analytics, and open science practices. The synthesis will clarify how mesoscale mitochondrial organization emerges and impacts cellular physiology.

title: Emergent Signaling Specificity: Integrating Single-Cell Phospho-Proteomics, Kinase Networks, and Imaging to Decode Pathway Crosstalk
abstract:
Cell signaling pathways exhibit emergent specificity: shared kinases and second messengers can yield distinct outcomes depending on context, timing, and spatial organization. Public datasets now include mass cytometry, single-cell phospho-proteomics, kinase-substrate maps, and live-cell imaging reporters, yet we lack a synthesis that explains how mesoscale organization and network context generate specific phenotypes.

This working group will integrate (i) single-cell phospho-signaling datasets (CyTOF and CITE-seq phospho panels with public deposition), (ii) bulk phosphoproteomics time courses (CPTAC, PRIDE), (iii) curated kinase-substrate relationships (PhosphoSitePlus, SIGNOR), (iv) protein interaction networks (BioGRID), (v) imaging datasets of signaling dynamics (IDR), and (vi) perturbation-response resources (LINCS, CRISPR screens). We will harmonize stimulation conditions, time points, and antibody/peptide mappings to comparable signaling features.

Scientific questions: (1) What network motifs and baseline states determine whether signals propagate linearly, saturate, oscillate, or bifurcate into distinct cell fates? (2) How does spatial compartmentalization (membrane microdomains, endosomes, nucleus) shape emergent pathway crosstalk? (3) Can we predict context-specific drug responses from integrated signaling state representations?

Methodologically, we will develop dynamical models that integrate time-resolved phosphoproteomics with single-cell heterogeneity. We will use latent variable ODE models and neural differential equations constrained by known kinase-substrate graphs to infer effective signaling circuits. Imaging-derived spatial features (e.g., nuclear translocation dynamics) will serve as additional constraints. A major deliverable will be a standardized benchmark for signaling model inference across modalities and a set of open tools for harmonizing phospho datasets.

NCEMS support is required because cross-modal integration of phospho data is technically challenging (inconsistent identifiers, variable coverage) and demands collaboration among proteomics experts, signaling biologists, statisticians, and ML researchers. The project’s community-scale nature includes building shared standards for metadata and reproducible pipelines.

Deliverables will include an open Signaling Specificity Atlas with harmonized datasets, inferred context-specific circuits, and predictive models of perturbation outcomes; reusable workflows for phosphoproteomics processing and integration; and tutorials for trainees on dynamical modeling and reproducible analysis. By synthesizing diverse public data, the project will uncover emergent principles explaining how cells achieve specific decisions using shared signaling components.

title: A Comparative Synthesis of Ribosome Heterogeneity and Specialized Translation Across Tissues and Stress Conditions
abstract:
Ribosomes are often treated as uniform machines, yet accumulating evidence suggests ribosome composition and rRNA modifications vary, potentially enabling specialized translation—an emergent regulatory layer at the mesoscale. Public datasets include ribosome profiling, quantitative proteomics of ribosomal proteins, rRNA modification maps, and genetic perturbations, but they have not been synthesized to test whether ribosome heterogeneity systematically predicts selective translation programs.

This working group will integrate (i) ribosome profiling datasets across tissues, development, and stress (GEO), (ii) proteomics quantifying ribosomal protein paralogs and associated factors (PRIDE, CPTAC), (iii) rRNA modification and ribosome biogenesis datasets (public epitranscriptomic studies), (iv) single-cell RNA-seq atlases for tissue context (Tabula Sapiens, HCA), and (v) perturbation datasets targeting ribosomal proteins, snoRNPs, and biogenesis factors (CRISPR screens, DepMap). We will curate metadata on growth conditions, stressors, and cell types, and standardize processing of ribosome profiling to comparable translation efficiency metrics.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify reproducible axes of ribosome heterogeneity (protein composition, modification patterns, associated factors) across contexts. (2) Test whether specific heterogeneity signatures correlate with selective translation of mRNA subsets (e.g., IRES-containing, uORF-rich, mitochondrial-targeted). (3) Determine whether specialized translation is conserved across species and how it relates to stress adaptation and disease.

Analytical approach: We will build joint models linking ribosome composition proxies (from proteomics and expression of ribosomal paralogs/biogenesis factors) to translation efficiency changes inferred from ribosome profiling. We will use multivariate association methods with careful confounder control (growth rate, global translation shifts) and causal inference leveraging perturbation datasets. We will also develop motif-based and structure-aware predictors of mRNAs sensitive to ribosome state.

NCEMS support is essential because integrating ribosome profiling with proteomics and modification data requires specialized expertise and substantial curation; no single lab typically spans these domains. The working group will coordinate standards for reporting ribosome profiling processing and for mapping ribosomal protein isoforms across datasets.

Deliverables will include a Ribosome Heterogeneity Synthesis Resource with harmonized datasets, inferred heterogeneity axes, and candidate specialized translation programs; reproducible pipelines for ribosome profiling processing; and open benchmarks for detecting specialized translation. Training will be provided through workshops on ribosome profiling analysis, proteomics integration, and open science practices, with trainees leading curation of tissue- and stress-specific modules. The synthesis will clarify whether and how ribosome diversity yields emergent translational control.

title: Emergent Properties of Membrane Microdomains: Integrating Lipidomics, Proteomics, and Super-Resolution Imaging of Raft-Like Assemblies
abstract:
Membrane microdomains (often described as lipid rafts) are proposed mesoscale assemblies that organize signaling and trafficking, yet their existence and functional roles remain debated due to methodological variability. Public lipidomics, proteomics, and imaging datasets provide an opportunity for a rigorous synthesis to identify when microdomains emerge, what compositions they exhibit, and how they influence cellular outcomes.

This working group will integrate (i) lipidomics datasets across cell types and perturbations (Metabolomics Workbench), (ii) membrane fractionation and detergent-resistant membrane proteomics (PRIDE), (iii) super-resolution and single-particle tracking imaging datasets that quantify nanoscale clustering (IDR), (iv) protein palmitoylation and other lipidation resources (SwissPalm, curated PTM databases), (v) perturbation datasets affecting cholesterol/sphingolipid metabolism and signaling (GEO, LINCS), and (vi) interaction networks for membrane proteins (BioGRID). We will curate experimental conditions to distinguish biochemical artifacts from consistent signals.

Scientific questions: (1) Are there reproducible compositional signatures of raft-like assemblies across methods, or are observed domains primarily assay-dependent? (2) Which lipid and protein features predict propensity to form mesoscale clusters (lipidation, transmembrane domain properties, oligomerization)? (3) How do microdomain states modulate emergent signaling behaviors such as ultrasensitivity and receptor crosstalk?

Methodologically, we will develop a cross-assay harmonization framework that models each experimental modality’s biases and extracts latent microdomain states. For imaging, we will standardize clustering metrics (Ripley’s K, pair correlation, cluster lifetime) and implement reproducible pipelines. For lipidomics/proteomics, we will map species and proteins to common ontologies and quantify co-enrichment patterns. Integrative models will connect inferred microdomain states to signaling outputs measured in phospho datasets or transcriptional responses.

NCEMS support is essential to convene lipid biochemists, membrane biophysicists, imaging experts, and data scientists to define standards and evaluate claims with transparent, reproducible analyses. The synthesis requires community-scale effort to curate heterogeneous datasets and build robust meta-analytic models.

Deliverables will include an open Membrane Microdomain Evidence Map with modality-specific and integrated confidence scores; standardized analysis workflows for super-resolution clustering and lipidomics integration; and predictive models linking composition to signaling phenotypes. Training will include modules on lipidomics normalization, spatial statistics for imaging, and open, reproducible meta-analysis. This project will resolve long-standing debates by grounding microdomain concepts in integrated, quantitative synthesis.

title: A Multi-Scale Synthesis of Endocytic Trafficking Emergence: From Coat Assembly to Organelle Identity
abstract:
Endocytic trafficking is an emergent system in which local coat assembly and cargo selection generate mesoscale organelles (early/late endosomes) with distinct identities and dynamic maturation. Public datasets include time-resolved imaging, proteomics of endosomal fractions, interaction networks, and perturbation screens, but they have not been unified to understand how organelle identity emerges from molecular interactions.

This working group will integrate (i) imaging datasets tracking endocytic markers and cargo trafficking (IDR, Cell Image Library), (ii) proteomics and phosphoproteomics of endosomal compartments and coat proteins (PRIDE), (iii) interaction networks for adaptors, Rab GTPases, and ESCRT machinery (BioGRID, SIGNOR), (iv) genome-wide perturbation screens affecting trafficking and receptor recycling (CRISPR screens, RNAi datasets), and (v) transcriptomic responses to trafficking perturbations (GEO). We will curate time-course information and experimental contexts (ligand stimulation, inhibitors) to enable dynamic inference.

Scientific aims: (1) Define conserved modules that specify endosomal identity and quantify how these modules assemble and transition over time. (2) Identify emergent checkpoints and bifurcation points that determine cargo fate (recycling vs degradation). (3) Determine how perturbations rewire trafficking networks to produce disease-relevant phenotypes (e.g., altered receptor signaling, lysosomal storage signatures).

Analytical approach: We will develop dynamic network models combining time-lapse imaging-derived trajectories (marker intensity and co-localization over time) with proteomic composition changes. Hidden Markov models and state-space approaches will infer discrete trafficking states and transition probabilities. Perturbation data will be used to assign causal roles to regulators. A methodological deliverable will be a standardized set of trafficking state features and open tools for extracting them from imaging.

NCEMS support is required to coordinate experts in membrane trafficking, quantitative imaging, proteomics, and dynamical modeling, and to host collaborative curation and benchmarking efforts. The scope—integrating many datasets across modalities and building dynamic inference tools—exceeds individual lab capacity.

Deliverables will include an open Endocytic Emergence Atlas describing trafficking states, modules, and transition maps; reproducible workflows for imaging trajectory extraction and proteomics integration; and a catalog of predicted regulators controlling cargo fate decisions. Training will include hands-on workshops on image-based time-series analysis, network modeling, and open science. This synthesis will reveal how mesoscale organelle identities and trafficking behaviors emerge from molecular-scale interactions.

title: Emergent Control of Cell Cycle Transitions: Integrating Single-Cell Time Series, Proteomics, and Perturbation Screens
abstract:
Cell cycle progression is governed by an emergent regulatory system where cyclin-CDK networks, checkpoints, and proteolysis create robust, irreversible transitions. Despite extensive study, open questions remain about how variability arises, how transitions differ across cell types, and which network features ensure irreversibility. Public single-cell time series, proteomics, and perturbation datasets provide an opportunity for a synthesis-driven advance.

This working group will integrate (i) single-cell RNA-seq datasets with cell cycle phase annotations across tissues and conditions (HCA, Tabula Sapiens, GEO), (ii) live-cell imaging time series of cell cycle reporters (IDR), (iii) quantitative proteomics and phosphoproteomics across cell cycle stages (CPTAC, PRIDE), (iv) ubiquitin-proteasome pathway datasets and degron perturbation time courses (GEO), and (v) CRISPR screens for cell cycle regulators (DepMap, published screens). We will harmonize phase labels using standardized markers and latent phase inference methods.

Scientific questions: (1) Which molecular features (phosphorylation waves, proteolysis timing, feedback loops) best explain emergent irreversibility of transitions (G1/S, G2/M)? (2) How do different cell types tune the same core network to yield distinct cycle lengths and checkpoint sensitivities? (3) Can we predict conditions that push the system toward critical slowing down or catastrophic arrest?

Analytical plan: We will construct integrated dynamical models combining single-cell trajectories (pseudotime/real time) with proteomic and phosphoproteomic dynamics. We will compare mechanistic models (bistable switches, coupled oscillators) using Bayesian model selection informed by multi-omic constraints. Perturbation screen results will provide causal anchors to identify key control nodes and to validate predicted sensitivities.

NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis requires coordinated expertise across cell cycle biology, quantitative imaging, proteomics, and dynamical systems modeling, as well as substantial infrastructure for harmonizing large datasets. The working group will establish community standards for cell cycle metadata and for integrating time-resolved omics.

Deliverables will include an open Cell Cycle Emergence Resource with harmonized datasets, inferred dynamic parameters, and comparative models across cell types; reproducible pipelines for phase inference and time alignment; and a catalog of predicted regulators governing variability and irreversibility. Training will include workshops on dynamical modeling, single-cell trajectory analysis, and reproducible workflows, with trainees leading dataset curation and benchmark construction. The synthesis will deepen understanding of how robust cell cycle control emerges from molecular interactions.

title: A Synthesis of Nuclear Body Emergence: Integrating Proteomics, RNA Localization, and Imaging of Speckles, Nucleoli, and PML Bodies
abstract:
Nuclear bodies (nucleoli, speckles, PML bodies, Cajal bodies) are mesoscale assemblies with emergent behaviors such as selective sequestration, reaction acceleration, and dynamic remodeling. While many components are known, we lack a unified synthesis linking composition, RNA content, and physical properties to nuclear functions across cell types and stresses.

This working group will integrate (i) proximity labeling and fractionation proteomics of nuclear bodies (PRIDE), (ii) RNA localization and interactome datasets (ENCODE eCLIP, RNA interactome capture studies), (iii) imaging datasets with nuclear body markers across tissues and perturbations (Human Protein Atlas, IDR), (iv) transcriptomic responses to stresses that remodel nuclear bodies (GEO), and (v) sequence/structure features of nuclear body proteins (disorder, low complexity, RNA-binding domains; AlphaFold and annotations). We will curate nuclear body types, experimental assays, and perturbation contexts.

Scientific questions: (1) What compositional “core” is conserved for each nuclear body type, and what peripheral components are condition-specific? (2) How do RNA species contribute to assembly and emergent function—are there common RNA features that promote nuclear body localization? (3) Can we relate nuclear body remodeling to changes in splicing, ribosome biogenesis, DNA repair, or antiviral responses?

Analytical approach: We will build a nuclear body knowledge graph combining protein–protein and protein–RNA interactions with imaging-derived co-localization and abundance features. Community detection will identify modules and condition-specific recruitment. We will develop predictive models for nuclear body targeting from sequence features and interaction context, and link remodeling signatures to functional outputs using transcriptomic and splicing analyses.

NCEMS support is required because the synthesis spans proteomics, RNA biology, imaging, and computational graph modeling, and demands coordinated curation across many studies. The working group will establish shared ontologies and data standards for nuclear body annotation.

Deliverables will include an open Nuclear Body Emergence Atlas with curated components, RNA associations, and remodeling signatures; reproducible workflows for integrating proteomics, eCLIP, and imaging; and benchmarks for predicting nuclear body localization. Training will include trainee-led curation sprints, tutorials on interaction network integration, and reproducible splicing analysis pipelines. The synthesis will reveal general principles by which mesoscale nuclear assemblies emerge and regulate genome function.

title: Emergent Antibiotic Tolerance Mechanisms: Synthesizing Bacterial Single-Cell Physiology, Transcriptomics, and Metabolic Models
abstract:
Antibiotic tolerance and persistence are emergent bacterial phenotypes where subpopulations survive lethal drugs without genetic resistance, often via metabolic slowdown, stress responses, and heterogeneous expression. Public datasets include single-cell time-lapse microscopy, transcriptomics under antibiotic stress, and genome-scale metabolic models, yet they remain disconnected. This working group will synthesize these data to uncover general principles of tolerance emergence across species and antibiotics.

We will integrate (i) single-cell imaging datasets tracking growth and survival under antibiotics (public microscopy repositories and supplemental datasets), (ii) bulk and single-cell bacterial transcriptomics under drug exposure (GEO), (iii) proteomics and metabolomics under antibiotic stress (PRIDE, Metabolomics Workbench), (iv) curated regulatory networks and stress response pathways (RegulonDB for E. coli, organism-specific resources), and (v) genome-scale metabolic models (BiGG) and flux data where available. We will standardize antibiotic classes, dosing regimens, growth media, and time points.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify conserved tolerance states characterized by coupled metabolic and regulatory signatures. (2) Determine whether tolerance arises via common dynamical motifs (bet-hedging, bistability, toxin–antitoxin modules) across species. (3) Link emergent single-cell survival distributions to underlying network states and metabolic constraints.

Analytical approach: We will combine stochastic dynamical modeling with data-driven state inference. Single-cell trajectories will be analyzed to infer phenotypic state transitions (growth arrest, recovery) and their rates. Transcriptomics/proteomics will define molecular correlates of these states. Constraint-based metabolic modeling will test whether inferred states correspond to distinct feasible flux regimes, and to predict metabolic interventions that collapse tolerance.

NCEMS support is essential because the synthesis requires coordinated expertise in microbiology, single-cell imaging analysis, systems biology, and stochastic modeling, plus extensive curation of heterogeneous experimental conditions. The working group will create shared standards for reporting tolerance imaging experiments and for mapping them to omics data.

Deliverables will include an open Antibiotic Tolerance Synthesis Atlas with harmonized single-cell and omics datasets, inferred tolerance states, and model-based predictions; reproducible pipelines for analyzing survival time series; and benchmarks for tolerance state classification. Training will include workshops on single-cell bacterial image analysis, metabolic modeling, and open science practices. This synthesis will advance fundamental understanding of how emergent phenotypes arise from molecular networks and may inform strategies to mitigate tolerance using existing data.

title: A Cross-Species Synthesis of Autophagosome Biogenesis: Integrating Proteomics, Lipid Signatures, and Imaging Dynamics
abstract:
Autophagy is a conserved process where emergent mesoscale structures—phagophores and autophagosomes—form, expand, and fuse with lysosomes. While core ATG proteins are known, puzzles remain about how initiation sites are selected, how membrane sources contribute, and how dynamics vary across species and stresses. Public imaging, proteomics, and lipidomics datasets offer a path to a community-scale synthesis.

This working group will integrate (i) live-cell imaging datasets of autophagy markers (LC3/Atg8, WIPI, ATG proteins) under diverse perturbations (IDR), (ii) proteomics of autophagosomes and ATG complexes (PRIDE), (iii) lipidomics datasets capturing PI3P and membrane lipid remodeling under autophagy induction (Metabolomics Workbench), (iv) interaction networks and PTM data for autophagy regulators (BioGRID, PhosphoSitePlus), and (v) genetic screens for autophagy factors across organisms (yeast, Drosophila, human CRISPR screens). We will curate stressors (starvation, ER stress, infection mimics) and annotate assay types.

Scientific questions: (1) What are conserved versus context-specific modules controlling autophagosome nucleation and expansion? (2) How do lipid remodeling signatures correlate with autophagosome morphology and formation rates? (3) Can we predict emergent autophagy dynamics (bursting vs steady-state) from upstream signaling and membrane source availability?

Analytical approach: We will extract quantitative dynamic features from imaging (puncta initiation rates, growth kinetics, fusion events) using standardized tracking pipelines. Multi-omic integration will link these features to proteomic composition and lipid signatures using latent factor models. Comparative analysis across species will identify conserved emergent behaviors and map divergence to specific regulatory innovations.

NCEMS support is required to coordinate autophagy biologists, lipidomics experts, quantitative imaging scientists, and computational modelers, and to host collaborative curation of heterogeneous datasets. The project’s scale and need for cross-modal harmonization exceed individual lab capabilities.

Deliverables will include an open Autophagosome Biogenesis Atlas with harmonized imaging-derived dynamics, proteomic modules, and lipid signatures; reproducible workflows for autophagy image tracking and omics integration; and a catalog of predicted regulators controlling dynamic regimes. Training will include hands-on workshops on image tracking, lipidomics normalization, and open science, with trainees leading dataset annotation and benchmark creation. The synthesis will yield general principles of how mesoscale autophagic structures emerge from molecular interactions.

title: Emergent RNA Localization Codes: Synthesizing Subcellular Transcriptomics, RBP Binding Maps, and Imaging to Predict RNA Destinations
abstract:
RNA localization creates mesoscale organization of gene expression, enabling local translation and compartment-specific regulation. Although many RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) and localization elements are known, a generalizable “localization code” remains elusive. Public datasets now include subcellular fractionation RNA-seq, APEX-seq, spatial transcriptomics, RBP binding maps (eCLIP), and RNA imaging—ideal for synthesis.

This working group will integrate (i) subcellular RNA localization datasets (APEX-seq, fractionation RNA-seq in GEO), (ii) eCLIP and related RBP binding maps (ENCODE), (iii) RNA modification data (m6A and others) where available, (iv) imaging datasets of RNA localization (MERFISH/FISH images in IDR and publications), (v) proteomics/localization for RBPs (HPA, PRIDE), and (vi) perturbation datasets altering RBPs or transport machinery (CRISPR screens, knockdown RNA-seq). We will harmonize compartment definitions (mitochondria, ER, nucleus subdomains, protrusions) and build a standardized annotation schema.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify sequence/structure motifs and RBP combinations that predict RNA localization across compartments and cell types. (2) Determine how localization programs change under stress (e.g., stress granule recruitment, ER stress) and differentiation. (3) Link emergent localization patterns to functional outputs such as localized translation and organelle proteome maintenance.

Analytical approach: We will develop multi-task predictive models that map RNA sequence features (UTR motifs, secondary structure, codon usage) plus RBP binding profiles to localization probabilities. Graph-based models will capture combinatorial RBP interactions. Imaging data will provide validation and refine compartment boundaries. We will also perform meta-analyses to quantify reproducibility and context dependence of localization signals.

NCEMS support is essential because integrating diverse RNA localization assays requires coordinated expertise in RNA biology, spatial transcriptomics, imaging, and machine learning, as well as substantial curation to align compartments and experimental contexts. The working group will establish community standards for reporting localization experiments and derived labels.

Deliverables will include an open RNA Localization Synthesis Database with harmonized labels and features; reproducible pipelines for processing APEX-seq/fractionation datasets; and predictive models with interpretable motif and RBP attributions. Training will include workshops on RNA motif modeling, eCLIP processing, and reproducible ML, with trainees leading curation of specific compartments. The synthesis will advance understanding of emergent spatial gene regulation at the mesoscale.

title: A Community Meta-Analysis of Multivesicular Body and Exosome Biogenesis: Integrating ESCRT Networks, Proteomics, and Imaging
abstract:
Extracellular vesicles (EVs), including exosomes, arise from multivesicular body (MVB) biogenesis—an emergent process where ESCRT machinery and lipid remodeling generate intraluminal vesicles and selective cargo loading. Although EV proteomics datasets are abundant, reproducibility is challenged by isolation variability, and mechanistic links between ESCRT network states and EV cargo remain unclear. This working group will synthesize public data to identify robust principles of MVB/EV emergence.

We will integrate (i) EV proteomics and RNA cargo datasets from community repositories (e.g., Vesiclepedia/ExoCarta-linked studies and PRIDE where raw data exist), (ii) proteomics and interaction networks of ESCRT components and accessory factors (PRIDE, BioGRID), (iii) imaging datasets of MVB formation and ESCRT dynamics (IDR), (iv) lipidomics related to ceramide and endosomal lipids (Metabolomics Workbench), and (v) perturbation datasets targeting ESCRT genes and endosomal regulators (CRISPR screens, GEO transcriptomics). We will curate EV isolation methods and develop metadata standards to enable stratified analyses.

Scientific questions: (1) What EV cargo signatures are robust across isolation methods and cell types, and which are artifacts? (2) How do ESCRT network configurations and lipid states influence emergent cargo selection and vesicle size distributions? (3) Are there conserved modules that couple endosomal trafficking with EV secretion under stress and disease states?

Analytical approach: We will perform hierarchical meta-analysis to separate biological signal from technical variation, explicitly modeling isolation method effects. Network-based integration will link cargo proteins to ESCRT interaction modules and endosomal localization evidence. Imaging-derived phenotypes (MVB number, ESCRT puncta dynamics) will be integrated to connect molecular modules to mesoscale organelle behavior. We will also develop classifiers that predict EV cargo enrichment from cellular proteome and trafficking state.

NCEMS support is essential because the EV field’s heterogeneity demands community coordination to build consensus standards and to curate large numbers of datasets. Expertise spanning endosomal biology, proteomics, lipidomics, imaging, and statistics is required.

Deliverables will include an open EV/MVB Synthesis Resource with standardized metadata, robust cargo signatures, and inferred mechanistic modules; reproducible pipelines for EV proteomics reanalysis; and guidelines for interpreting public EV datasets. Training will include trainee-led curation of EV datasets, workshops on meta-analysis and batch-effect modeling, and open science practices. This synthesis will clarify how mesoscale MVB processes generate emergent extracellular communication vehicles.

title: Emergent Mechanics of the Nucleus: Integrating Lamin Variants, Chromatin State, and Microscopy-Based Deformation Phenotypes
abstract:
Nuclear mechanics emerge from interactions between lamins, chromatin, and cytoskeletal coupling, influencing migration, genome stability, and differentiation. Public datasets include lamin isoform expression, chromatin state maps, high-content imaging of nuclear shape, and mechanical perturbation assays, yet they have not been synthesized to derive general principles linking molecular composition to emergent mechanical phenotypes.

This working group will integrate (i) imaging datasets quantifying nuclear morphology across perturbations (Cell Painting, IDR, HPA), (ii) transcriptomic and proteomic profiles of lamins and nuclear envelope components across tissues (GTEx-like expression resources, CPTAC), (iii) epigenomic maps reflecting chromatin compaction (ENCODE ATAC-seq/ChIP-seq), (iv) perturbation datasets altering lamins, chromatin modifiers, and LINC complex components (CRISPR screens, GEO), and (v) datasets reporting nuclear deformation under confinement or strain where raw imaging is public. We will standardize nuclear shape descriptors (eccentricity, blebbing, wrinkling) and infer mechanical proxies from deformation assays.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify molecular determinants of emergent nuclear stiffness and deformability across cell types. (2) Determine how chromatin compaction states interact with lamin composition to produce nonlinear mechanical responses and failure modes (rupture). (3) Link nuclear mechanical states to downstream outcomes such as DNA damage signatures, transcriptional changes, and migration phenotypes.

Analytical approach: We will build integrative models combining imaging-derived mechanical proxies with omics features. Mechanistic modeling will incorporate composite material concepts (lamina shell + chromatin core) to interpret data-driven relationships. We will use causal inference leveraging perturbations to disentangle lamin-driven versus chromatin-driven effects. A methodological deliverable will be an open toolkit for extracting standardized nuclear mechanics features from microscopy images.

NCEMS support is required because the synthesis spans mechanobiology, imaging analytics, epigenomics, and statistical modeling, and demands coordinated curation across diverse datasets. The working group will establish metadata standards for nuclear mechanics experiments and promote reusable analysis pipelines.

Deliverables will include a Nuclear Mechanics Emergence Atlas with harmonized imaging features, molecular predictors, and inferred mechanical regimes; reproducible workflows for nuclear shape and deformation analysis; and a catalog of candidate regulators of rupture susceptibility. Training will include workshops on quantitative image analysis, mechanistic modeling, and open science. The synthesis will elucidate how mesoscale nuclear mechanics emerge from molecular and chromatin organization.

title: A Synthesis of Spatially Structured Immune Synapse Formation: Integrating Imaging, Proteomics, and Signaling Perturbation Data
abstract:
The immune synapse is a mesoscale, spatially patterned interface where receptors, adhesion molecules, and cytoskeletal structures self-organize to enable antigen recognition and signaling. Despite extensive study, we lack a unified synthesis connecting molecular composition, spatial patterning, and emergent signaling outcomes across immune cell types and stimulation contexts. Public imaging and omics datasets can now be integrated to address this gap.

This working group will integrate (i) high-resolution imaging datasets of immune synapses (TCR/BCR clustering, actin organization) from IDR and published repositories, (ii) proteomics of immunological synapse fractions and signaling complexes (PRIDE), (iii) phospho-signaling time courses following receptor stimulation (PRIDE/CPTAC/GEO), (iv) interaction networks and curated signaling pathways (SIGNOR, BioGRID), and (v) perturbation datasets (CRISPR screens, inhibitor panels, LINCS-like perturbation transcriptomics in immune contexts). We will standardize stimulation conditions (ligand potency, mechanical context) and extract quantitative spatial metrics (cluster size distributions, radial organization, actin ring integrity).

Scientific aims: (1) Identify conserved spatial organization motifs and relate them to signaling amplitude, duration, and specificity. (2) Determine how cytoskeletal and membrane organization constraints produce emergent thresholds for activation. (3) Compare synapse organization across T cells, B cells, NK cells, and engineered CAR-T contexts to identify generalizable design principles.

Analytical approach: We will develop models that couple spatial statistics from imaging with dynamical signaling models. Graph-based representations of synapse architecture will be linked to phospho-signaling trajectories using multimodal learning. Perturbation data will provide causal anchors to identify regulators controlling spatial patterning and signaling outcomes. A methodological deliverable will be an open, standardized pipeline for immune synapse image quantification.

NCEMS support is essential to convene immunologists, imaging experts, proteomics specialists, and computational modelers, and to coordinate curation and benchmarking across heterogeneous datasets. The project’s community-scale integration is beyond a single lab’s scope.

Deliverables will include an Immune Synapse Emergence Atlas with harmonized spatial metrics, molecular modules, and predicted activation regimes; reproducible workflows for synapse image analysis and signaling integration; and a catalog of candidate targets that modulate synapse organization. Training will be provided through workshops on spatial image analysis, signaling modeling, and open science practices, with trainees leading dataset annotation and tool development. This synthesis will reveal how mesoscale spatial self-organization drives emergent immune decision-making.

title: Emergent Principles of Protein Allostery at Scale: Integrating Structural Ensembles, Mutational Scans, and Functional Genomics
abstract:
Allostery—long-range coupling between sites in proteins—is an emergent property of molecular structure and dynamics. While classic studies focus on individual proteins, public deep mutational scanning (DMS), structural models, and functional genomics now enable a synthesis to identify general rules predicting allosteric coupling and its cellular consequences.

This working group will integrate (i) DMS datasets with publicly available raw/processed scores (MaveDB), (ii) structural data and predicted models (PDB, AlphaFold DB), (iii) molecular dynamics ensemble resources where available, (iv) protein interaction and pathway context (BioGRID, Reactome), and (v) human genetic variation and disease annotations (gnomAD, ClinVar) to connect allosteric sites to phenotypes. We will curate protein families with multiple DMS studies to enable comparative analyses.

Scientific aims: (1) Identify structural and sequence determinants of allosteric sensitivity (e.g., network centrality in residue contact graphs, flexibility, packing frustration). (2) Quantify how allosteric coupling patterns vary across protein classes (enzymes, transcription factors, membrane receptors) and evolutionary distances. (3) Link predicted allosteric sites to cellular phenotypes via pathway integration and genetic dependency data, illuminating why certain distal variants are pathogenic.

Analytical approach: We will compute residue interaction networks from structures and develop models that predict mutational effects at distal sites using graph neural networks and interpretable network metrics. We will meta-analyze DMS across conditions to detect context-dependent allostery. Integrating functional genomics (e.g., dependency scores) will allow prioritization of allosteric sites most relevant to cellular fitness. A methodological deliverable will be an open benchmark suite for allostery prediction using standardized splits across proteins and families.

NCEMS support is required because the synthesis spans structural biology, statistical genetics, ML, and systems biology, and requires coordinated curation of diverse DMS experiments and structural representations. The working group will align on standards for mapping DMS variants to structures and for reporting uncertainty.

Deliverables will include an open Allostery Synthesis Atlas with harmonized DMS-to-structure mappings, predicted allosteric networks, and links to disease variants; reproducible pipelines for feature extraction and modeling; and benchmarks for community method development. Training will include workshops on structural data processing, DMS analysis, and reproducible ML, with trainees leading curation of protein families. The synthesis will uncover general emergent rules of allostery and enable better interpretation of distal variants.

title: Deciphering the Sequence-to-Emergent-Property Grammar of Biomolecular Condensates
abstract: The emergence of biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation represents a paradigm shift in understanding mesoscale cellular organization. Despite extensive single-lab studies, the universal predictive rules governing how diverse protein and RNA sequences encode the physical properties of these condensates remain elusive. This mesoscale phenomenon bridges the gap between nanoscale molecular interactions and macroscale cellular functions, such as stress response and gene expression. Understanding this emergence is critical for solving long-standing puzzles in molecular and cellular biosciences, specifically regarding how non-membrane-bound organelles dynamically assemble and disassemble in response to environmental cues. Current research is highly fragmented, lacking a unified framework to explain how local interactions scale up to form functional, mesoscale structures that dictate global cellular outcomes. To address this, our working group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decipher the sequence-to-emergent-property grammar of phase separation. By integrating publicly available proteomics data, single-molecule biophysics datasets, transcriptomics, and high-throughput imaging repositories from the Protein Data Bank, LLPSDB, and the Image Data Resource, we will employ advanced artificial intelligence and machine learning frameworks to model condensate emergence. Our approach utilizes graph neural networks and deep learning architectures to synthesize these disparate multi-omics and imaging datasets, entirely bypassing the need for new experimental data. This innovative analytical strategy will allow us to map the multidimensional landscape of phase separation, identifying hidden patterns and emergent properties that cannot be observed in isolated datasets. The proposed synthesis goes far beyond the capacity of any individual laboratory, necessitating the dedicated support and resources of NCEMS. We will convene a transdisciplinary team of structural biologists, biophysicists, computational scientists, and cell biologists. Our working group is intentionally assembled to reflect diverse scientific perspectives, career stages, geographic locations, and institutional research levels, ensuring a robust and inclusive approach to this complex problem. This collaborative partnership will break down traditional disciplinary silos, fostering a dynamic environment where diverse new talent can thrive. Crucially, the project serves as a premier training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will be co-mentored across disciplines, gaining hands-on experience in cloud computing, AI-driven data integration, and collaborative research methodologies. In strict adherence to open science principles, all synthesized datasets, AI models, and analytical pipelines will be made freely available to the broader scientific community through open-source repositories like GitHub and Zenodo. Ultimately, this project reveals how the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale influences higher-order cellular functions.

title: Emergence of Cellular Morphology from Cytoskeletal Crosstalk and Motor Protein Dynamics
abstract: The dynamic interplay between actin filaments and microtubules drives the emergence of complex cellular morphologies, representing a fundamental example of mesoscale biological organization. While the individual components of the cytoskeleton have been studied exhaustively, the emergent properties arising from their large-scale crosstalk remain a critical puzzle in cellular biomechanics. This mesoscale emergence dictates essential cellular outcomes, including directed migration, division, and mechanosensing. Understanding how these distinct biopolymer networks coordinate via crosslinking proteins and molecular motors to generate global cellular forces is essential for advancing our knowledge of cellular emergence. Currently, the field lacks a comprehensive model that integrates molecular-level motor kinetics with whole-cell morphological changes. To bridge this gap, our working group proposes a transdisciplinary synthesis project to decode the emergent mechanics of cytoskeletal crosstalk. We will aggregate and synthesize publicly available cryo-electron tomography datasets, live-cell super-resolution microscopy archives, and biophysical force-measurement databases from repositories such as EMPIAR and the Cell Image Library. By leveraging topological data analysis and agent-based machine learning models, we will simulate and analyze the emergent network topologies without generating any new experimental data. This data science approach will identify the universal principles by which local cytoskeletal interactions produce global, mesoscale cellular architectures. Addressing this multi-scale problem requires resources and collaborative infrastructure that far exceed the capabilities of a single research group, making NCEMS support indispensable. Our working group will unite a diverse cohort of polymer physicists, structural biologists, computational mechanobiologists, and live-cell imaging experts. We have specifically recruited team members from various geographic locations and institutional backgrounds to ensure a wide range of scientific perspectives. This diversity will stimulate cross-disciplinary innovation, allowing us to tackle this long-standing puzzle from multiple angles. Furthermore, this project is deeply committed to training the next generation of researchers. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive unparalleled cross-training in computational modeling, big data synthesis, and complex systems theory. By working in a highly collaborative team, trainees will develop the skills necessary to lead the future of data-savvy biological research. We are fully committed to gold-standard open science practices; all integrated datasets, simulation codebases, and analytical workflows will be published openly via Zenodo and GitHub. Through this synthesis, we will illuminate how nanoscale molecular motors and biopolymers orchestrate the unexpected appearance of mesoscale forces, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS mission to uncover the fundamental rules of biological emergence.

title: Synthesizing the Emergent Properties of Chromatin Topology and Epigenetic Memory
abstract: The three-dimensional folding of the genome into topologically associating domains represents a profound example of mesoscale emergence that fundamentally regulates gene expression and cellular identity. While one-dimensional epigenetic marks and isolated chromatin looping events are well-documented, the rules governing how these local interactions scale up to form stable, mesoscale chromatin architectures remain a major unresolved puzzle. This emergence of higher-order chromatin structure from linear DNA sequences and localized protein binding dictates critical subcellular outcomes, including cell fate determination and epigenetic memory. The lack of a unified understanding of this mesoscale phenomenon stems from the historical siloing of genomic, structural, and transcriptomic data. Our working group proposes a community-scale data synthesis initiative to resolve the emergent properties of chromatin topology. We will systematically integrate massive volumes of publicly available Hi-C, ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and RNA-seq data from international consortia such as ENCODE, the 4D Nucleome Project, and the Gene Expression Omnibus.
