By employing advanced transformer-based deep learning models and graph convolutional networks, we will synthesize these distinct, multi-omics datasets to predict the emergence of 3D chromatin structures from 1D sequence data, entirely utilizing existing public data. This innovative analytical strategy will uncover the hidden grammar of mesoscale genome organization. The sheer volume and complexity of this multi-omics integration necessitate the unique collaborative environment and computational resources provided by NCEMS. No single laboratory possesses the interdisciplinary expertise required to bridge genomics, polymer physics, and advanced artificial intelligence. Our team brings together computational genomicists, biophysicists, machine learning engineers, and developmental biologists from diverse institutions and career stages. This collaborative partnership will tap into diverse new talent, fostering an inclusive environment that drives novel scientific insights. A core component of our proposal is the rigorous training of the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in a transdisciplinary mentoring network, acquiring highly sought-after skills in deep learning, genomic data science, and reproducible research workflows. We will strictly adhere to community-created policies on open science, ensuring that all code, trained AI models, and synthesized chromatin interaction maps are freely accessible via public repositories. By synthesizing these vast public datasets, our working group will reveal how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale chromatin domains influences global transcriptional programs, thereby answering long-standing questions about the physical basis of epigenetic memory and cellular emergence.

title: Emergence of Metabolic Adaptation through Mitochondrial Reticular Network Dynamics
abstract: Mitochondria are not isolated organelles but exist as dynamic, interconnected reticular networks whose emergent properties dictate cellular metabolism, apoptosis, and stress resistance. The continuous cycle of mitochondrial fusion and fission creates a mesoscale network that is highly responsive to environmental cues. However, the exact mechanisms by which localized protein interactions at the mitochondrial membrane scale up to alter the global topology and metabolic output of the entire network remain a fundamental mystery in cellular biology. Understanding this mesoscale emergence is crucial for deciphering how cells dynamically adapt their energy production to meet fluctuating demands. Our working group aims to solve this long-standing puzzle through a community-scale synthesis of mitochondrial dynamics. We will integrate diverse, publicly available datasets, including high-resolution volumetric electron microscopy from the OpenOrganelle database, live-cell fluorescence imaging from the Image Data Resource, and comprehensive metabolomics profiles from the Metabolomics Workbench. To analyze this complex, multi-modal data without generating new experiments, we will develop novel computer vision algorithms and spatial network analysis tools. Using reinforcement learning and deep neural networks, we will model how local fusion and fission events cascade to produce emergent, cell-wide metabolic states. This project requires the integration of structural imaging with functional metabolomics at a scale that is impossible for a single research lab, making the support of NCEMS absolutely vital. We will assemble a transdisciplinary team comprising cell biologists, network theorists, computer vision experts, and metabolic modelers. title: Decoding the Mesoscale Emergence of Lipid Raft Clustering and Transmembrane Signaling

title: Uncovering the Rules of Nucleolar Assembly and Ribosome Biogenesis Emergence

We will integrate publicly available glycomics, spatial transcriptomics, and super-resolution imaging datasets from specialized repositories like GlyTouCan, the Gene Expression Omnibus, and the Image Data Resource. By employing advanced graph neural networks and spatio-temporal deep learning architectures, we will model the dynamic network of glycan interactions without generating any new experimental data. This innovative data science approach will identify the universal principles by which local sugar biosynthesis leads to the mesoscale emergence of functional cellular barriers. The complexity of glycobiology requires the integration of chemical biology with multi-omics data, a task that demands the collaborative infrastructure provided by NCEMS. Our transdisciplinary working group unites glycobiologists, computational biophysicists, multi-omics experts, and machine learning engineers. We have prioritized diverse scientific perspectives by recruiting team members from various career stages, geographic locations, and institutional backgrounds. This diversity will foster a dynamic environment capable of generating novel insights into complex cellular surface networks. Training the next generation of researchers is a central focus of our initiative. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive rigorous cross-training in big data integration, AI-driven pattern recognition, and collaborative open science workflows. We commit to making all analytical pipelines, synthesized datasets, and predictive models publicly accessible via Zenodo and GitHub, ensuring full reproducibility. By synthesizing existing public data, this project will answer fundamental questions about how cells orchestrate the unexpected appearance of mesoscale surface barriers, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS mission to catalyze discoveries in cellular emergence.

title: Emergent Contractility from Myosin II Thick Filament Assembly in Non-Muscle Cells
abstract: In non-muscle cells, the dynamic assembly of non-muscle myosin II into mesoscale bipolar thick filaments is essential for generating the contractile forces that drive cell migration, adhesion, and cytokinesis. The transition from individual, auto-inhibited myosin motors to highly ordered, force-generating mesoscale ensembles represents a classic example of biophysical emergence. However, the precise spatio-temporal rules governing how localized phosphorylation events and actin network architecture coordinate to drive this large-scale filament assembly remain a highly debated puzzle in mechanobiology. Understanding this emergence is vital for deciphering how cells dynamically alter their shape and exert physical force. Our working group proposes a comprehensive data synthesis project to decode the emergent properties of myosin filament assembly. We will integrate diverse, publicly available datasets, including live-cell super-resolution microscopy, biophysical force measurements, and phosphoproteomics from repositories such as the Cell Image Library, PRIDE, and specific mechanobiology databases. By utilizing advanced spatio-temporal data mining and unsupervised machine learning algorithms, we will synthesize these distinct datasets to identify the universal principles of mesoscale contractility. This approach relies entirely on existing data, leveraging AI to uncover the hidden rules of how local molecular motors scale up to produce global cellular forces. The multifaceted nature of cellular biomechanics requires a collaborative partnership that transcends individual lab capabilities, making NCEMS support essential. We will convene a transdisciplinary team of mechanobiologists, structural biophysicists, computational modelers, and data scientists. Our working group is structured to promote diverse scientific perspectives, incorporating researchers from various geographic locations, institutional types, and career stages. This inclusive environment will stimulate the cross-disciplinary innovation necessary to solve this critical biological mystery. Training the future data-savvy workforce is a core component of our mission. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in a collaborative network, gaining expertise in multi-modal data integration, AI-driven network analysis, and open science protocols. We commit to making all findings, integrated databases, and analytical workflows publicly accessible via community-standard repositories like GitHub. By synthesizing these vast public datasets, our project will reveal how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale contractile structures influences higher-order cellular morphology, directly supporting the NCEMS vision of understanding biological emergence.

title: Decoding the Emergent Dynamics of Proteasome Clustering and Localized Degradation
abstract: The ubiquitin-proteasome system is the primary mechanism for targeted protein degradation in eukaryotic cells. Recent evidence suggests that under certain conditions, proteasomes dynamically cluster into mesoscale condensates to efficiently process high localized concentrations of ubiquitinated substrates. This emergent spatial organization represents a paradigm shift from the traditional view of freely diffusing proteasomes. However, the biophysical drivers of this mesoscale clustering and how it dictates the global efficiency of cellular protein quality control remain a fundamental, unsolved puzzle. Understanding this emergence is crucial for explaining how cells maintain proteostasis during stress and aging. Our working group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decipher the emergent properties of proteasome clustering. We will systematically integrate publicly available spatial proteomics data, live-cell fluorescence imaging, and interactomic datasets from the PRIDE database, the Image Data Resource, and BioGRID. By employing advanced computer vision algorithms and spatial network analysis tools powered by machine learning, we will synthesize these disparate datasets to model the dynamic state of the proteasome network. This approach utilizes only existing public data to develop innovative analytical strategies that reveal the physical rules of mesoscale degradation emergence. The sheer scale and complexity of integrating spatial imaging with functional proteomics require the robust collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS. Our transdisciplinary team brings together cell biologists, protein biochemists, computational data scientists, and systems biologists. We have intentionally assembled a working group that reflects diverse scientific perspectives, including researchers from various career stages and geographic locations. This diversity is essential for breaking down disciplinary silos and fostering novel insights into complex biological phenomena. Training the next generation of researchers is a fundamental aspect of our proposal. Trainees will receive cross-disciplinary mentorship, developing critical skills in spatial bioinformatics, AI-driven modeling, and collaborative open science. In strict adherence to community policies on reproducible science, all integrated datasets, network models, and analytical code will be published openly via Zenodo and GitHub. By synthesizing structural and functional data, this project will illuminate how the unexpected appearance of mesoscale organelle networks influences higher-order cellular proteostasis, perfectly aligning with the overarching goals of NCEMS.

title: Synthesizing the Emergent Meshwork of the Nuclear Lamina and Genome Tethering
abstract: The nuclear lamina is a dense, mesoscale meshwork of intermediate filaments located at the inner nuclear membrane. It provides essential structural integrity to the nucleus and serves as a critical tethering platform for organizing peripheral heterochromatin. The assembly of individual lamin proteins into this complex, highly ordered mesoscale architecture, and how this structure dynamically responds to mechanical stress, is a profound example of cellular emergence. Despite its importance in gene regulation and mechanobiology, the precise rules governing lamina meshwork assembly and its emergent impact on 3D genome topology remain poorly understood. Our working group proposes a transdisciplinary synthesis project to decode the emergent biophysics of the nuclear lamina. We will aggregate and synthesize massive, publicly available datasets, including super-resolution localization microscopy, Hi-C genomic data, and cryo-electron tomography from repositories such as the 4D Nucleome Project, EMPIAR, and the Image Data Resource. By utilizing advanced topological data analysis and spatio-temporal deep learning architectures, we will synthesize these multi-modal datasets to reconstruct the dynamic architecture of the lamina without generating any new experimental data. This innovative data science approach will identify the universal principles by which local protein polymerization leads to the mesoscale emergence of functional nuclear barriers. The complexity of nuclear biophysics requires the integration of structural imaging with genomic data, a task that demands the collaborative infrastructure provided by NCEMS. Our transdisciplinary working group unites nuclear biologists, computational biophysicists, genomicists, and machine learning engineers. We have prioritized diverse scientific perspectives by recruiting team members from various career stages, geographic locations, and institutional backgrounds. This diversity will foster a dynamic environment capable of generating novel insights into complex nuclear networks. Training the next generation of researchers is a central focus of our initiative. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will receive rigorous cross-training in big data integration, AI-driven pattern recognition, and collaborative open science workflows. We commit to making all analytical pipelines, synthesized datasets, and predictive models publicly accessible via Zenodo and GitHub, ensuring full reproducibility. By synthesizing existing public data, this project will answer fundamental questions about how cells orchestrate the unexpected appearance of mesoscale nuclear structures, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS mission to catalyze discoveries in cellular emergence.

title: Decoding the Emergent Logic of Phase-Separated Condensates: A Multi-Scale Data Synthesis of Biomolecular Organization Principles
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates represent a paradigm shift in our understanding of cellular organization, yet the rules governing their emergent properties remain poorly understood. This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary team spanning structural biology, biophysics, computational biology, and systems biology to synthesize publicly available data across multiple scales to decode the organizational logic of phase-separated condensates. Our central hypothesis is that condensate properties emerge from predictable combinations of molecular features that can be identified through systematic integration of structural, sequence, interaction, and cellular imaging data.

We will integrate data from multiple public repositories including the Protein Data Bank (PDB), AlphaFold Database, PhaSePro, DrLLPS, STRING, BioGRID, and the Human Protein Atlas. Additionally, we will leverage cryo-electron tomography datasets from EMPIAR and single-molecule tracking data from public repositories. This integration spans molecular structure, protein-protein interactions, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modifications, and cellular localization patterns.

Our approach involves three interconnected aims. First, we will develop a comprehensive atlas of condensate-forming proteins by synthesizing sequence features, structural properties, and interaction networks. Machine learning approaches will identify molecular grammar rules that predict condensate formation propensity and material properties. Second, we will analyze spatial and temporal dynamics of condensates by integrating live-cell imaging datasets with proteomics and transcriptomics data to understand how condensate composition and properties respond to cellular states and perturbations. Third, we will construct multi-scale models linking molecular features to mesoscale organization and cellular function.

The project requires NCEMS support because it demands expertise spanning structural biology, bioinformatics, machine learning, biophysics, and cell biology that no single laboratory possesses. The data integration challenge alone requires computational infrastructure and expertise in harmonizing heterogeneous data types. Our team includes researchers from five institutions across three geographic regions, incorporating faculty at different career stages and from primarily undergraduate institutions.

Expected outcomes include: (1) a publicly available database linking molecular features to condensate properties, (2) predictive models for condensate behavior, (3) new hypotheses about condensate function testable by the broader community, and (4) analytical workflows for multi-scale data integration. All analysis code, integrated datasets, and findings will be made publicly available following FAIR principles.

Training is central to our mission. Graduate students and postdocs will participate in cross-laboratory exchanges, learning diverse computational and analytical approaches. We will host virtual workshops teaching data synthesis methods to the broader community. This project addresses a fundamental question in cellular organization: how do molecular properties give rise to mesoscale structures with emergent functions? By synthesizing existing data at unprecedented scale, we will generate insights impossible for individual laboratories and establish frameworks for future synthesis research in cellular organization.

title: Temporal Emergence in Protein Interaction Networks: Synthesizing Dynamic Interactomics Across Cell Cycle, Circadian, and Stress Response Programs
abstract:
Protein interaction networks are not static entities but dynamically rewire across time, yet most network analyses treat interactions as fixed. This proposal addresses a fundamental gap: understanding how temporal dynamics of protein interactions give rise to emergent cellular behaviors. We hypothesize that time-dependent network rewiring follows predictable patterns that enable cells to transition between functional states, and that these patterns can be decoded through synthesis of existing temporal proteomics, interactomics, and transcriptomics datasets.

Our multidisciplinary team brings together network scientists, systems biologists, chronobiologists, and computational biologists from six institutions to synthesize publicly available temporal datasets spanning cell cycle progression, circadian rhythms, and stress responses. We will integrate data from PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, GEO, ArrayExpress, BioGRID, IntAct, and published time-series studies. This includes phosphoproteomics capturing signaling dynamics, protein abundance measurements, interaction mapping studies, and single-cell RNA sequencing time courses.

The project pursues three synergistic aims. First, we will construct temporal protein interaction networks by integrating time-resolved proteomics with static interaction data, developing computational methods to infer interaction dynamics from protein abundance and modification changes. Second, we will identify conserved network motifs and rewiring patterns across different temporal programs, testing whether cells employ common strategies for network reorganization. Third, we will develop predictive models linking network dynamics to emergent cellular phenotypes such as cell division, metabolic switching, and stress adaptation.

This synthesis project requires NCEMS support for several reasons. The data integration challenge spans multiple data types, organisms, and experimental conditions requiring diverse expertise. No single laboratory has the breadth of knowledge needed to interpret patterns across cell cycle biology, circadian biology, and stress biology. The computational infrastructure for analyzing dynamic networks at this scale exceeds typical laboratory resources.

Our team composition reflects NCEMS values: researchers from R1 universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, and international collaborators; faculty spanning assistant to full professor ranks; and strong representation of early-career researchers. Geographic diversity spans East Coast, Midwest, and West Coast institutions.

Deliverables include: (1) a temporal protein interaction database with visualization tools, (2) software for inferring interaction dynamics from proteomics data, (3) a catalog of conserved network rewiring motifs, and (4) mechanistic models of temporal emergence. All resources will be publicly released with comprehensive documentation.

Training opportunities include graduate student rotations between laboratories, a summer workshop on temporal network analysis, and mentored research experiences for undergraduates from partner institutions. This project will establish foundational principles for understanding how molecular interaction dynamics give rise to emergent cellular behaviors across time.

title: The Mesoscale Architecture of Mitochondrial Contact Sites: Integrating Structural, Proteomic, and Functional Data to Understand Emergent Organelle Communication
abstract:
Membrane contact sites between mitochondria and other organelles represent critical hubs for cellular homeostasis, yet how their mesoscale architecture enables emergent functions in calcium signaling, lipid transfer, and metabolic regulation remains mysterious. This proposal unites structural biologists, mitochondrial biologists, lipidomics experts, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode the organizational principles of mitochondrial contact sites and their functional consequences.

Mitochondria-ER contact sites (MERCs), mitochondria-lysosome contacts, and mitochondria-lipid droplet interfaces each possess distinct protein compositions and functions, but comprehensive understanding of their architecture-function relationships is lacking. We will integrate cryo-electron tomography data from EMPIAR revealing contact site ultrastructure, proteomics data from proximity labeling studies, lipidomics datasets, calcium imaging data, and metabolomics measurements. Cross-referencing with disease-associated variants from ClinVar and GWAS catalogs will connect molecular architecture to physiological relevance.

Our first aim develops an integrated structural model of mitochondrial contact sites by synthesizing tomography data with protein structural predictions from AlphaFold and experimentally determined structures from PDB. We will map protein complexes to contact site architectures and identify organizational principles. Our second aim connects contact site composition to function by integrating proteomics, lipidomics, and metabolomics data across cell types and conditions. Machine learning approaches will identify compositional signatures predicting functional outcomes. Our third aim examines how contact site dysfunction contributes to disease by linking architectural and compositional features to disease phenotypes.

This project exemplifies the need for NCEMS support. Understanding contact sites requires expertise spanning membrane biology, structural biology, metabolism, and computational modeling that no single laboratory encompasses. Data integration across imaging, proteomics, and metabolomics modalities requires specialized computational approaches. The collaborative framework enables synthesis impossible through traditional single-laboratory efforts.

Our team includes researchers from seven institutions, spanning structural biology, mitochondrial biology, computational biology, and metabolism. Career stages range from assistant professors to senior investigators, with strong participation from underrepresented groups and primarily undergraduate institutions.

Expected outcomes include: (1) an integrated database of mitochondrial contact site architecture and composition, (2) predictive models linking contact site features to cellular functions, (3) identification of disease-relevant contact site alterations, and (4) new hypotheses for experimental validation. All data integration workflows, analysis code, and findings will be publicly released.

Training is embedded throughout the project. Graduate students will gain experience in multi-modal data integration through collaborative research. Postdocs will develop leadership skills through aim coordination. We will develop educational modules on contact site biology and data synthesis methods for the broader community. This project will establish principles for understanding how mesoscale organelle interfaces enable emergent cellular functions.

title: Emergent Properties of the Cellular Crowding Landscape: Synthesizing Biophysical, Structural, and Systems Data to Understand Macromolecular Organization
abstract:
The cellular interior is extraordinarily crowded, with macromolecules occupying 20-40% of cytoplasmic volume, yet how this crowding influences molecular behavior and gives rise to emergent cellular properties remains poorly understood. This proposal assembles biophysicists, structural biologists, systems biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode how crowding shapes cellular organization and function at the mesoscale.

Macromolecular crowding affects protein folding, diffusion, interaction kinetics, and phase behavior, but these effects have been studied in isolation. We hypothesize that integrating diverse data types will reveal emergent organizational principles arising from crowding that cannot be understood from any single data source. Our synthesis will integrate protein abundance data from PaxDb and proteomics repositories, structural data from PDB and AlphaFold, diffusion measurements from FRAP and single-molecule tracking studies, and spatial proteomics data from the Human Protein Atlas and subcellular fractionation studies.

Our first aim constructs a quantitative map of the cellular crowding landscape by integrating protein abundance, size, and localization data to estimate local crowding across subcellular compartments. We will develop computational models predicting how crowding varies spatially and temporally. Our second aim synthesizes biophysical measurements to understand how crowding affects molecular behavior, integrating diffusion coefficients, binding constants, and reaction rates measured under different crowding conditions. Our third aim connects crowding to emergent cellular phenomena including phase separation, reaction compartmentalization, and metabolic channeling.

This project requires NCEMS support because it demands integration of biophysical, structural, and systems-level data requiring expertise no single laboratory possesses. The challenge of connecting molecular-scale crowding effects to cellular-scale organization requires collaborative efforts spanning multiple disciplines. Computational infrastructure for modeling crowded cellular environments exceeds typical laboratory capabilities.

Our team spans eight institutions across four countries, including biophysicists, structural biologists, systems biologists, and computational scientists. We include researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions and community colleges, ensuring broad participation and training opportunities.

Deliverables include: (1) a publicly available database of cellular crowding parameters across cell types and conditions, (2) computational tools for predicting crowding effects on molecular behavior, (3) models connecting crowding to emergent cellular organization, and (4) educational resources on crowding biology. All analysis workflows and findings will be openly shared.

Training opportunities include graduate student exchanges between biophysics and systems biology laboratories, workshops on integrating biophysical and omics data, and research experiences for undergraduate students. This project addresses a fundamental question: how does the crowded cellular environment shape emergent biological organization? By synthesizing diverse data types, we will establish principles for understanding mesoscale cellular organization.

title: Deciphering the Emergence of Cellular Polarity: Multi-Scale Data Synthesis Across Molecular, Mesoscale, and Cellular Organization
abstract:
Cellular polarity—the asymmetric organization of cellular components—is essential for development, tissue function, and disease prevention, yet how molecular interactions give rise to this emergent mesoscale organization remains incompletely understood. This proposal brings together cell biologists, developmental biologists, physicists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data spanning molecular interactions to tissue-level organization to decode the principles underlying polarity emergence.

Polarity establishment involves coordinated action of conserved protein modules including PAR proteins, Rho GTPases, and phosphoinositides, but how these molecular components self-organize into stable asymmetric distributions is poorly understood. We will integrate protein interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct, structural data from PDB and AlphaFold, imaging data from public repositories, single-cell transcriptomics from GEO and Human Cell Atlas, and spatial transcriptomics datasets. Cross-species comparisons will identify conserved principles.

Our first aim synthesizes molecular interaction networks underlying polarity, integrating protein-protein interactions, lipid-protein interactions, and post-translational modifications to construct comprehensive polarity networks. Our second aim examines mesoscale organization by integrating super-resolution imaging data, electron microscopy datasets, and proximity labeling proteomics to understand how molecular interactions produce asymmetric protein distributions. Our third aim connects molecular and mesoscale organization to cellular and tissue-level polarity phenotypes by integrating imaging, transcriptomics, and phenotypic data.

This synthesis project requires NCEMS support for multiple reasons. Understanding polarity emergence requires expertise spanning molecular biology, cell biology, developmental biology, physics, and computational modeling. Data integration across imaging modalities, proteomics, and transcriptomics demands specialized computational approaches. The collaborative framework enables insights impossible through individual laboratory efforts.

Our team includes researchers from six institutions spanning cell biology, developmental biology, biophysics, and computational biology. We include faculty from primarily undergraduate institutions and researchers at various career stages, ensuring diverse perspectives and training opportunities.

Expected outcomes include: (1) comprehensive polarity interaction networks across species, (2) models linking molecular interactions to mesoscale organization, (3) identification of conserved principles and species-specific adaptations, and (4) predictions for experimental validation. All integrated datasets, analysis workflows, and findings will be publicly released following FAIR principles.

Training is central to our project. Graduate students will participate in cross-laboratory research, gaining experience in diverse methodologies. We will develop educational modules on polarity biology and multi-scale data integration. Summer workshops will train the broader community in synthesis approaches. This project will establish foundational principles for understanding how molecular interactions give rise to emergent cellular asymmetry.

title: The Grammar of Intrinsically Disordered Regions: Synthesizing Sequence, Structure, and Function Data to Predict Emergent Behaviors
abstract:
Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) comprise approximately 30% of eukaryotic proteomes and are central to cellular regulation, signaling, and organization, yet predicting their functional behaviors from sequence remains challenging. This proposal unites structural biologists, bioinformaticians, biophysicists, and cell biologists to synthesize publicly available data to decode the sequence-function grammar of IDRs and predict their emergent behaviors including phase separation, protein interactions, and regulatory functions.

IDRs lack stable three-dimensional structures but adopt transient conformational ensembles that enable diverse functions. Current understanding of IDR function is fragmented across disparate studies. We will integrate sequence databases, structural ensembles from NMR and molecular dynamics simulations, phase separation propensity data, post-translational modification annotations, interaction data, and cellular localization information. This comprehensive synthesis will reveal principles connecting IDR sequence features to functional outcomes.

Our first aim develops a comprehensive IDR feature database by synthesizing sequence annotations, predicted and experimental structural ensembles, and biophysical properties. We will apply machine learning to identify sequence patterns associated with specific functions. Our second aim connects IDR features to interaction behaviors by integrating protein-protein interaction data, binding site annotations, and structural data on IDR-mediated complexes. Our third aim links IDR properties to emergent cellular behaviors including condensate formation, signaling hub function, and transcriptional regulation.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding IDR function requires expertise spanning bioinformatics, structural biology, biophysics, and cell biology that no single laboratory possesses. The data integration challenge—connecting sequence features to cellular functions—requires diverse computational approaches and biological insights. The scale of analysis exceeds typical laboratory capabilities.

Our team includes researchers from seven institutions spanning structural biology, bioinformatics, biophysics, and cell biology. We include early-career investigators, researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions, and international collaborators, ensuring diverse perspectives.

Deliverables include: (1) a comprehensive IDR feature database with visualization tools, (2) predictive models for IDR function from sequence, (3) identification of IDR grammar rules for specific functions, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released with comprehensive documentation.

Training opportunities include graduate student rotations between computational and experimental laboratories, workshops on IDR analysis methods, and research experiences for undergraduates. This project addresses a fundamental challenge in molecular biology: predicting protein function from sequence for the substantial fraction of proteins containing disordered regions. By synthesizing diverse data types, we will establish principles for understanding how IDR sequences encode emergent functional behaviors.

title: Emergent Organization of the Cytoskeletal Interactome: Integrating Structural, Dynamic, and Functional Data Across Actin, Microtubule, and Intermediate Filament Networks
abstract:
The cytoskeleton comprises interconnected networks of actin filaments, microtubules, and intermediate filaments that collectively enable cell shape, motility, and intracellular organization, yet how these systems interact to produce emergent mechanical and organizational properties remains poorly understood. This proposal assembles cytoskeleton biologists, biophysicists, structural biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode the organizational principles of the integrated cytoskeletal system.

Traditionally studied in isolation, the three cytoskeletal systems are increasingly recognized as functionally interconnected. Crosslinking proteins, motor proteins, and signaling molecules coordinate their behaviors, but comprehensive understanding of this integration is lacking. We will integrate structural data from PDB and cryo-EM repositories, protein interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct, live-cell imaging datasets, mechanical measurement data, and proteomics data from cytoskeletal preparations.

Our first aim constructs an integrated cytoskeletal interactome by synthesizing protein-protein interaction data, structural information, and localization data to map connections between cytoskeletal systems. We will identify hub proteins and regulatory nodes. Our second aim examines dynamic coordination by integrating time-resolved imaging data, single-molecule tracking studies, and perturbation experiments to understand how cytoskeletal systems communicate. Our third aim connects cytoskeletal organization to emergent cellular properties including mechanical behavior, organelle positioning, and cell migration.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding cytoskeletal integration requires expertise spanning actin biology, microtubule biology, intermediate filament biology, biophysics, and computational modeling. No single laboratory possesses this breadth. Data integration across imaging, structural, and proteomic modalities requires specialized computational approaches and infrastructure.

Our team includes researchers from eight institutions with expertise spanning all three cytoskeletal systems plus biophysics and computational biology. We include researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions and various career stages, ensuring diverse participation.

Expected outcomes include: (1) an integrated cytoskeletal interactome database, (2) models of cytoskeletal coordination and crosstalk, (3) identification of key regulatory nodes, and (4) predictions linking cytoskeletal organization to cellular behaviors. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student exchanges between laboratories studying different cytoskeletal systems, workshops on cytoskeletal data analysis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses a fundamental question in cell biology: how do interconnected cytoskeletal networks produce emergent cellular organization and mechanics? By synthesizing data across systems, we will establish principles for understanding mesoscale cytoskeletal organization.

title: Synthesizing the Spatiotemporal Logic of Post-Translational Modification Crosstalk: From Molecular Signals to Emergent Cellular Decisions
abstract:
Post-translational modifications (PTMs) including phosphorylation, ubiquitination, acetylation, and methylation regulate virtually all cellular processes, yet how combinatorial PTM patterns—the PTM code—encode cellular decisions remains poorly understood. This proposal unites proteomics experts, systems biologists, structural biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available PTM data to decode the spatiotemporal logic of PTM crosstalk and its role in emergent cellular behaviors.

Individual PTMs have been extensively catalogued, but understanding their combinatorial logic requires integration across data types and conditions. We will synthesize PTM data from PhosphoSitePlus, UniProt, PRIDE, and ProteomeXchange, structural data revealing PTM effects on protein conformation, interaction data showing PTM-dependent binding, and phenotypic data connecting PTM patterns to cellular outcomes. Time-resolved PTM datasets will reveal dynamic crosstalk patterns.

Our first aim constructs a comprehensive PTM crosstalk network by integrating data on co-occurring modifications, sequential modifications, and mutually exclusive modifications. We will identify recurring crosstalk motifs and their functional consequences. Our second aim examines spatial organization of PTM signaling by integrating subcellular proteomics with PTM data to understand compartment-specific modification patterns. Our third aim connects PTM patterns to emergent cellular decisions including cell cycle progression, differentiation, and stress responses.

This project requires NCEMS support because decoding PTM crosstalk requires expertise spanning proteomics, structural biology, signaling biology, and computational modeling. The data integration challenge—connecting molecular modifications to cellular outcomes—requires diverse approaches. The scale of analysis and computational requirements exceed typical laboratory capabilities.

Our team includes researchers from six institutions spanning proteomics, structural biology, systems biology, and computational biology. We include early-career investigators, researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions, and international collaborators.

Deliverables include: (1) a comprehensive PTM crosstalk database with visualization tools, (2) predictive models for PTM pattern outcomes, (3) identification of PTM code rules for specific cellular decisions, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student rotations between proteomics and computational laboratories, workshops on PTM data analysis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses a fundamental question in cell biology: how do combinatorial PTM patterns encode emergent cellular behaviors? By synthesizing diverse PTM data, we will establish principles for understanding the PTM code and its role in cellular decision-making.

title: The Emergent Architecture of Stress Granules: Multi-Modal Data Synthesis to Understand Assembly, Composition, and Function
abstract:
Stress granules are membraneless organelles that form in response to cellular stress, sequestering mRNAs and proteins to regulate gene expression, yet the principles governing their emergent properties remain incompletely understood. This proposal assembles RNA biologists, structural biologists, cell biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode stress granule organization and function.

Stress granules represent a paradigmatic example of mesoscale cellular organization, forming through phase separation of RNA-binding proteins and mRNAs. However, comprehensive understanding of their composition, dynamics, and functional consequences is lacking. We will integrate proteomics data from stress granule purifications, RNA sequencing data identifying granule-associated transcripts, structural data on component proteins, imaging data revealing granule dynamics, and phenotypic data connecting granule properties to cellular outcomes.

Our first aim constructs a comprehensive stress granule component database by synthesizing proteomics and RNA sequencing data across stress conditions, cell types, and organisms. We will identify core versus stress-specific components and predict new components. Our second aim examines stress granule architecture by integrating structural data, crosslinking mass spectrometry, and super-resolution imaging to understand internal organization. Our third aim connects stress granule properties to functional outcomes by integrating composition data with transcriptomics, translatomics, and phenotypic measurements.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding stress granules requires expertise spanning RNA biology, protein biochemistry, structural biology, and cell biology. Data integration across proteomics, transcriptomics, and imaging modalities requires specialized computational approaches. The collaborative framework enables insights impossible through individual laboratory efforts.

Our team includes researchers from seven institutions spanning RNA biology, structural biology, cell biology, and computational biology. We include researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions and various career stages.

Expected outcomes include: (1) a comprehensive stress granule component database, (2) models of stress granule architecture and assembly, (3) identification of functional modules within granules, and (4) predictions linking granule properties to cellular stress responses. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student exchanges between laboratories, workshops on membraneless organelle analysis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about mesoscale cellular organization: how do stress granules assemble, what determines their composition, and how do their emergent properties influence cellular stress responses?

title: Decoding Emergent Metabolic Channeling: Synthesizing Structural, Interaction, and Flux Data to Understand Metabolon Organization
abstract:
Metabolic enzymes often organize into transient complexes called metabolons that channel substrates between sequential reactions, yet the principles governing metabolon formation and their emergent effects on cellular metabolism remain poorly understood. This proposal unites structural biologists, metabolic biochemists, systems biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode metabolon organization and function.

Metabolic channeling enhances pathway efficiency and enables regulatory control, but metabolons are challenging to study due to their transient nature. We will integrate protein interaction data from BioGRID, IntAct, and proximity labeling studies, structural data from PDB and AlphaFold, metabolomics data from MetaboLights and Metabolomics Workbench, flux measurements, and subcellular localization data. Cross-species comparisons will identify conserved channeling principles.

Our first aim maps the metabolon interaction landscape by synthesizing protein-protein interaction data for metabolic enzymes across pathways and organisms. We will identify recurring interaction patterns and predict new metabolon components. Our second aim examines metabolon architecture by integrating structural data with interaction information to model how enzymes organize for substrate channeling. Our third aim connects metabolon organization to emergent metabolic properties by integrating interaction data with flux measurements and metabolomics to understand how channeling affects pathway behavior.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding metabolons requires expertise spanning structural biology, enzymology, systems biology, and computational modeling. Data integration across interaction, structural, and metabolic data types requires diverse approaches. The collaborative framework enables comprehensive analysis impossible for individual laboratories.

Our team includes researchers from six institutions spanning structural biology, biochemistry, systems biology, and computational biology. We include early-career investigators and researchers from primarily undergraduate institutions.

Deliverables include: (1) a metabolon interaction database, (2) structural models of metabolon organization, (3) predictive models linking metabolon formation to metabolic outcomes, and (4) hypotheses for experimental validation. All resources will be publicly released.

Training opportunities include graduate student rotations between structural and systems biology laboratories, workshops on metabolon analysis, and undergraduate research experiences. This project addresses fundamental questions about metabolic organization: how do enzymes organize into metabolons, and how does this mesoscale organization produce emergent metabolic properties?

title: The Emergence of Ribosome Heterogeneity: Synthesizing Structural, Compositional, and Translational Data to Understand Specialized Ribosomes
abstract:
Ribosomes were long considered uniform molecular machines, but emerging evidence suggests compositional heterogeneity enabling specialized translation, yet the principles governing ribosome specialization and its functional consequences remain poorly understood. This proposal assembles structural biologists, translation biologists, systems biologists, and computational scientists to synthesize publicly available data to decode ribosome heterogeneity and its emergent effects on gene expression.

Ribosome heterogeneity arises from differential incorporation of ribosomal protein paralogs, ribosomal RNA modifications, and associated factors. We will integrate structural data from PDB and EMDB, ribosome profiling data from GEO, proteomics data on ribosome composition, RNA modification data, and translation efficiency measurements. Cross-species and cross-tissue comparisons will reveal conserved and specialized features.

Our first aim maps ribosome compositional diversity by synthesizing proteomics data on ribosomal protein composition across cell types, tissues, and conditions. We will identify patterns of paralog usage and associated factors. Our second aim examines structural consequences of compositional variation by integrating structural data with compositional information to understand how heterogeneity affects ribosome architecture. Our third aim connects ribosome heterogeneity to emergent translational properties by integrating compositional data with ribosome profiling and translation efficiency measurements.

This project requires NCEMS support because understanding ribosome heterogeneity requires expertise spanning structural biology, translation biology, and systems biology. Data integration across structural, proteomic, and functional data types requires specialized approaches. title: Emergent Properties of the Nuclear Pore Complex: Integrating Structural, Transport, and Regulatory Data Across Scales
abstract:
